Solving a system

Source: vignettes/solvers.Rmd
solvers.Rmd

Installation 

install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/linop")

Installing linop installs one package. There are no Imports and no compiled code, so there is no toolchain to have working first. Matrix sits in Suggests and is used for sparse leaves and as_sparse().

R 4.4.0 or newer. The floor is set by crossprod() and tcrossprod(), which became S3 generic in R 4.4.0, and are what let one matrixOps method cover all three matrix products.

One verb

solve() is R’s generic for a x = b, and a linop has a method for it. There is no second verb to learn and no separate object to construct.

n <- 200
L <- linop(
  function(X) 2 * X - rbind(X[-1, , drop = FALSE], 0) - rbind(0, X[-n, , drop = FALSE]),
  dim = c(n, n)
)
xstar <- sin(seq_len(n) * pi / (n + 1))
b <- as.numeric(L %*% xstar)

x <- solve(L, b)
max(abs(x - xstar))
#> [1] 1.061568e-12

L is the 1D Laplacian written as its action. Nothing was factorized, because for an operator given as a closure there is nothing to factorize. What came back is a plain numeric vector, so it indexes and multiplies like any other, and it carries a record of how it was produced:

attr(x, "certificate")
#> solved by gmres (no capability is established, and gmres requires none)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> arithmetic floor               pass         computation      estimate              -
#> residual                       pass         computation      identity              1
#> backward error                 pass         computation      estimate              -
#> convergence                    pass         computation      identity              1
#> forward error                  not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        qualified   no deterministic bound on: arithmetic floor, backward error, forward error

The first line is the one to read here. The rest of that table is the subject of vignette("certificates").

What auto chose, and why

method = "auto" picks from what the operator has established about itself and from its shape, and records both the choice and the reason. Three routes are reachable.

A diagonal operator of full rank is solved exactly, with no iteration at all:

D <- linop_scaling(seq(1, 4, length.out = 50))
attr(solve(D, rep(1, 50)), "certificate")$dispatch$reason
#> [1] "the operator is diagonal and of full rank, so the solve is exact"

A dense leaf checks its own symmetry when it is built, on data it already holds, so a symmetric matrix reaches MINRES:

M <- crossprod(matrix(rnorm(60 * 60), 60, 60)) + diag(60)
Ad <- linop(M)
bd <- as.numeric(Ad %*% rep(1, 60))
attr(solve(Ad, bd), "certificate")$dispatch$reason
#> [1] "the operator is hermitian, and definiteness is not established"

The operator above is positive definite, and auto still chose MINRES rather than CG. Symmetry was computed; definiteness was not, and auto will not assume it. There is a CG branch above the MINRES one, and no constructor in the package currently reaches it, because the routes that establish definiteness at a source auto accepts are diagonal and are taken by the direct route first. CG is reached by naming it.

That is the general rule, and it applies to declarations too. L at the top of this article was built with no properties at all. Declaring them changes nothing about which method auto picks:

Ldecl <- linop(
  function(X) 2 * X - rbind(X[-1, , drop = FALSE], 0) - rbind(0, X[-n, , drop = FALSE]),
  dim = c(n, n),
  properties = c(hermitian = TRUE, positive_definite = TRUE)
)
attr(solve(Ldecl, b), "certificate")$dispatch$reason
#> [1] "no capability is established, and gmres requires none"

Both capabilities are TRUE and auto acted on neither, because a bare declaration is not the kind of argument auto will choose a method on. The capability and the evidence behind it are two separate questions, which is what vignette("capabilities") is about. Here it decides a dispatch.

GMRES is the fallback, and it is what makes auto total rather than partial: it requires nothing of the operator, and it runs on the forward action alone. L has no adjoint, which is why every route above it was unavailable in the first place.

Naming a method

Naming a method is the caller making the assertion, so no evidence minimum applies:

attr(solve(Ldecl, b, method = "cg"), "certificate")$dispatch
#> $requested
#> [1] "cg"
#> 
#> $chosen
#> [1] "cg"
#> 
#> $reason
#> [1] "named by the caller, so no evidence minimum was applied"

The declaration on Ldecl is true, CG is the right method for it, and saying so is how you get it. The two questions stay separate: auto is the package choosing on your behalf, and a named method is your own claim about your own operator.

A declaration that is false is not silently tolerated. CG forms p^H A p every step, and a value that is not positive far from convergence means the operator is not what it said it was, which is an error naming the capability rather than a wrong answer.

The seven methods

method requires adjoint shape
cg hermitian positive definite no square
minres hermitian no square
gmres nothing no square
fgmres nothing no square
bicgstab nothing no square
lsqr nothing yes any
lsmr nothing yes any

GMRES and BiCGSTAB both require nothing and both run without an adjoint. They are not interchangeable. GMRES minimises the residual over the whole Krylov space, so its residual cannot rise and it has no breakdown; BiCGSTAB is cheaper per step and can break down, in which case it returns a fail certificate naming the breakdown rather than throwing. auto prefers GMRES for the first reason.

FGMRES is GMRES with the one difference that it accepts a preconditioner that changes between applications, such as an inner iterative solve.

Least squares is a different request

solve() with method = "auto" refuses a rectangular operator, and says what to name instead:

G <- matrix(rnorm(120 * 40), 120, 40)
R <- linop(G)
bl <- rnorm(120)
solve(R, bl)
#> Error:
#> ! solve() needs a square operator; this one is 120 x 40.
#>   A rectangular system is a least-squares problem, min ||b - a x||, which is a
#>   different request rather than the same one on a different shape. Name the method
#>   to make it: solve(a, b, method = "lsqr") or method = "lsmr".

This is deliberate. min ||b - A x|| is a different mathematical question from A x = b, rather than the same one on a different shape, so the caller states which they meant. Both methods are reachable through the same verb:

xl <- solve(R, bl, method = "lsqr")
max(abs(xl - qr.solve(G, bl)))
#> [1] 3.203147e-09

LSQR and LSMR solve the same problem and minimise different things over the same bidiagonalisation. LSQR minimises ||r||. LSMR minimises ||A^H r||, which is the quantity that goes to zero at a least-squares solution and the numerator of the backward error the certificate reports:

xm <- solve(R, bl, method = "lsmr")
c(lsqr = attr(xl, "certificate")$values$backward_error,
  lsmr = attr(xm, "certificate")$values$backward_error)
#>         lsqr         lsmr 
#> 4.008744e-09 3.731806e-09

Preconditioners

A preconditioner is built from one direction, M^-1, and carries what it declares about itself:

set.seed(2)
d <- 10^runif(200, 0, 5)
Adense <- diag(d)
Adense[cbind(1:199, 2:200)] <- -1
Adense[cbind(2:200, 1:199)] <- -1
A <- linop(Adense)
xs <- rep(1, 200)
bb <- as.numeric(A %*% xs)

P <- preconditioner(function(R) R / d, hermitian = TRUE,
                    positive_definite = TRUE, side = "left", dim = c(200, 200))
P
#> <preconditioner>
#>   side:              left
#>   fixed:             TRUE
#>   hermitian:         TRUE
#>   positive_definite: TRUE
#>   M^-H:              equal to M^-1, by the hermitian declaration

The diagonal of that operator spans five orders of magnitude. At a fixed budget of 40 iterations, with everything else equal:

plain  <- solve(A, bb, method = "minres", maxit = 40, tol = 1e-10)
scaled <- solve(A, bb, method = "minres", maxit = 40, tol = 1e-10,
                preconditioner = P)

c(plain  = max(abs(plain  - xs)),
  scaled = max(abs(scaled - xs)))
#>        plain       scaled 
#> 1.007307e+00 1.294592e-07
c(plain  = attr(plain,  "certificate")$overall,
  scaled = attr(scaled, "certificate")$overall)
#>       plain      scaled 
#>      "fail" "qualified"

Each method states which properties it needs of a preconditioner and which sides it is defined for, and enforces both at the point the preconditioner is accepted:

method requires sides
cg fixed, hermitian, positive definite left, right, split
minres fixed, hermitian, positive definite left, right, split
gmres fixed left, right, split
fgmres nothing right
bicgstab fixed left, right, split
lsqr fixed right
lsmr fixed right

A refusal names what was missing:

flexible <- preconditioner(function(R) R / d, fixed = FALSE,
                           hermitian = TRUE, positive_definite = TRUE,
                           side = "left", dim = c(200, 200))
solve(A, bb, method = "minres", preconditioner = flexible)
#> Error:
#> ! method 'minres' requires a preconditioner with fixed = TRUE; this one has fixed = FALSE.
#>   A flexible preconditioner changes between applications; use fgmres, which takes a right-side preconditioner.

For CG the three sides coincide, so its row is unrestricted because the distinction does not arise. For GMRES all three are implemented and they produce different iterates, so its row is unrestricted for the opposite reason:

set.seed(1)
Gm <- matrix(rnorm(80 * 80), 80, 80)
diag(Gm) <- diag(Gm) + 12
Ag <- linop(Gm)
bg <- as.numeric(Ag %*% rep(1, 80))
dg <- diag(Gm)

vapply(c("left", "right", "split"), function(sd) {
  Ps <- preconditioner(function(R) R / dg, hermitian = TRUE,
                       positive_definite = TRUE, side = sd, dim = c(80, 80))
  attr(solve(Ag, bg, method = "gmres", maxit = 6, tol = 1e-12,
             preconditioner = Ps), "certificate")$values$residual
}, numeric(1))
#>       left      right      split 
#> 0.04805537 0.04799045 0.04800726

Right preconditioning minimises the residual that gets reported. Left and split minimise a preconditioned one, so the outer loop converts the target going in and measures in your units coming out.

The narrow rows are the two least-squares methods, and the reason is the shape. M^-1 acts on the domain of the operator; left and split act on the codomain, which for a rectangular operator is a different space.

A solve that does not converge

An exhausted budget is a result, not an exception. It comes back as a fail certificate that says what ran out:

attr(plain, "certificate")
#> solved by minres (named by the caller, so no evidence minimum was applied)
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> check                          status       source           guarantee             conf
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> arithmetic floor               pass         computation      identity              1
#> residual                       fail         computation      estimate              -
#> backward error                 fail         computation      estimate              -
#> convergence                    fail         computation      identity              1
#> forward error                  not_checked  computation      identity              -
#> ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> overall                        fail   no deterministic bound on: residual, backward error, forward error
#> 
#> failures:
#>   residual: worst ||b - A x|| / ||b|| = 7.135e-04 against tol 1.000e-10, floor 3.360e-15
#>   backward error: worst ||r|| / (||A|| ||x|| + ||b||) = 1.886e-04 against tol 1.000e-10
#>   convergence: 40 of at most 40 iterations; budget exhausted

The iterate is finite and usable, the number reached is reported, and nothing was thrown. A contradicted declaration is the case that does throw, because there the operator is not what it claimed and no iterate is worth returning.

details = TRUE returns the whole object rather than the solution, including the convergence history:

fit <- solve(A, bb, method = "minres", maxit = 40, tol = 1e-10, details = TRUE)
names(fit)
#>  [1] "x"           "certificate" "method"      "iterations"  "restarts"   
#>  [6] "converged"   "residual"    "history"     "requested"   "reason"
fit$iterations
#> [1] 40
fit$converged
#> [1] FALSE
